title: When the Bakery Falls
premise: Oscar Underhill inherited his family's failing vineyard along with its crushing debts, and he has spent ten years answering letters from a stranger who signed herself 'Wren' — the only tenderness in a life pared down to survival. When Wren, whose real name is Marguerite Bellamy, buys the abandoned cottage next door to finally meet him face to face, Oscar discovers she was hired years ago by his late mother to write hope into his life. Furious and undone, he must decide whether a love built on letters can survive the truth of why they were written — and whether the vineyard, or his heart, is worth saving when the harvest festival's last train offers her an escape from her own ruined past.
about_author: Ada Underhill is the pen name of a former sommelier who spent five harvest seasons in the Loire Valley before trading corkscrews for keyboards. She writes love stories set in places where the work is hard, the money is scarce, and the wine is honest.

chapters.title: The Last Good Barrel
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Opening on the eve of harvest, Oscar bottles what may be the vineyard's final vintage while creditors' letters pile beside one worn shoebox of decade-old correspondence from 'Wren.' He rereads her latest letter and almost writes back for the first time in a year. Emotional beat: quiet grief disguised as routine; the reader learns the vineyard and the letters are his only remaining attachments.

chapters.title: A Woman with Moving Boxes
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A rented truck pulls up at the derelict cottage adjoining his land, and its new owner introduces herself as Marguerite Bellamy — a book restorer escaping a failed marriage and a city that bankrupted her. Something about her cadence snags in Oscar's memory like a song half-remembered. Emotional beat: wary curiosity; two guarded people circling each other over a shared fence line.

chapters.title: What Wren Knew
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She unpacks her past and her guilt: ten years ago, dying and desperate, Oscar's mother paid her to write anonymous letters of encouragement to her son. Marguerite kept writing after the checks stopped because she fell in love with the man inside the letters. She has come to confess or to stay — she hasn't decided which. Emotional beat: longing braided with shame.

chapters.title: Pruning Season
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A storm damages the vines, and Marguerite shows up unasked with tarred hands and no complaints, working until dark. Over cheap wine afterward, their conversation has the eerie intimacy of people who already know each other's souls. He catches himself telling her things he never told anyone. Emotional beat: the first crack in his solitude; attraction he refuses to name.

chapters.title: The Shoebox on the Table
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Invited to dinner, Marguerite sees the shoebox of her own letters on Oscar's table and nearly confesses — but he mentions his mother's deathbed wish that 'someone would keep writing to him,' and the confession dies in her throat. She lies instead, saying she moved here for a fresh start. Emotional beat: dread compounding; every kindness now doubles as deception.

chapters.title: Debt Collectors and Dance Cards
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The bank gives Oscar thirty days before foreclosure unless the festival week's sales are extraordinary. Meanwhile the town assumes he and Marguerite are courting, and festival organizers rope them into co-chairing the harvest dance. Planning it together, banter turns electric, and Oscar realizes he is happy — a feeling so foreign it frightens him. Emotional beat: rising warmth against a ticking clock.

chapters.title: Postmarked Ten Years Ago
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Her estranged ex-husband arrives demanding money she doesn't have, threatening to expose her letter-writing scheme to Oscar if she won't pay. That night she finds Oscar asleep at his kitchen table, pen in hand, drafting a reply to Wren after all these years. She reads her own words over his shoulder and weeps silently. Emotional beat: the trap closing; love and blackmail converging.

chapters.title: The Truth, Spilled Like Wine
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At the festival's opening night, the ex-husband confronts Marguerite publicly, and Oscar pieces the truth together from fragments — then demands it outright. She admits everything: the payments, the letters, the decade of invented hope. Feeling mocked and mother-managed, Oscar tells her to leave on tomorrow's train. Emotional beat: climax of betrayal; the vineyard's fate and his heart both in freefall.

chapters.title: Reading Them Again
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Alone among the festival crowds, Oscar rereads all hundred-plus letters and sees what rage hid: the writer knew him, loved him, and stayed unpaid for nine years out of devotion, not duty. He finds her at the station platform as the last train idles, and instead of goodbye, he asks her to stay — not as Wren, but as Marguerite. Emotional beat: reversal and surrender; choosing the flawed real person over the perfect fiction.

chapters.title: After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The train leaves empty-handed but full-hearted. Weeks later, an anonymous buyer clears the vineyard's debt — revealed as Marguerite's savings and the sale of her restoration business. At the festival's closing night, under lanterns, Oscar pours the last good barrel and toasts 'to letters answered late.' She stays. Emotional beat: resolution; belonging earned honestly, love surviving the truth that nearly killed it.
